pile/memory: Linear attention's state is a memory from keys to values. Here key one, zero holds the value two, three, and key zero, one holds one, four.
pile/again: Now the first key comes back with a new value, four, one, as when a text changes a fact it gave before. Linear attention just adds another table.
pile/pile: Read that key now, and out comes six, four: the old value plus the new one, piled up. Nothing is ever overwritten.
pile/angle: And only keys at a right angle stay apart. A key between them, zero point six, zero point eight, reads back a mix of both values.
pile/cap: Keys of two numbers have room for only two directions at right angles. Store more pairs than a key has numbers, and the reads start to blend.
pile/schlag: In 2021, Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Yoorgen Schmidhoober pointed out both limits of linear attention, and a fix: before writing, read what the memory already holds.
delta/old: First, read what the memory holds for this key: S times k, here two, three. That is the old value.
delta/delta: Then take the difference between the new value and the old: four, one, minus two, three, is two, minus two. It is called the delta, after the Greek letter for a change.
delta/write: Write only that difference, as a table with the key: add the outer product of the delta and k.
delta/check: Read again: the old two, three, plus the delta, gives four, one. The new value replaces the old, instead of piling onto it.
delta/rule: That is the delta rule: S gets S, plus v minus S k, times k transpose.
delta/unit: The read moves by the delta times k dot k, so the value is replaced exactly when the key has length one. Today's models built on the rule scale every key to length one.
delta/other: A key at a right angle to k is left alone, since its dot product with k is zero: key zero, one still reads one, four.
beta/beta: One more piece: a write strength, beta, a number from zero to one that scales the difference before it is written.
beta/one: At one, the new value replaces the old: the key reads four, one.
beta/half: At a half, the read moves halfway, to three, two: a blend of old and new.
beta/zero: At zero, nothing is written, and the key still reads two, three.
beta/made: The model makes beta from each token, with learned weights and a sigmoid, so each token decides how firmly it is written.
learn/error: There is another way to see the rule. S times k is the memory's guess at v, and the guess minus v is its error.
learn/loss: Square the error's length and halve it, for a loss. Then take one step of gradient descent on it, with beta as the step size.
learn/grad: The loss's slope for the entry in row i, column j of S is the error's entry i, times k's entry j: the outer product. So the step adds minus beta, times the error, times k transpose: exactly the delta rule.
learn/widrow: The rule is old. In 1960, Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff trained adaptive circuits with it: nudge the weights by the error times the input, one example at a time.
learn/fast: So S is a set of weights that keeps learning while the model reads: fast weights, rewritten at every token, where the weights that make keys and values are slow, set in training. Hence Schlag's title: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers.
learn/deltanet: They called the model a Delta Network. In 2024, Songlin Yang and colleagues found how to train DeltaNet in parallel over a whole text, and at one point three billion parameters it beat other recurrent models of its size at predicting text.
